_comment: Military campaigns. Each is a schematic line from origin to target, visible only in its year (start == end). Shown with an animated dash. Sources: Assyrian/Babylonian annals, 2 Kings, Babylonian Chronicle.

popup.bible: Unmentioned — but Ahab of Israel is there, on the Kurkh Monolith, with 2,000 chariots.
popup.archaeology: The Battle of Qarqar: Shalmaneser III's march west meets an anti-Assyrian coalition led by Damascus, including 'Ahab the Israelite' — the largest chariot force recorded in the inscription.

popup.bible: The Assyrian king who takes Damascus and strips Galilee and Gilead from Israel (2 Kgs 15:29) — the beginning of the end.
popup.archaeology: Tiglath-Pileser III's annals list the conquest of Damascus and the deportation of its people; the northern kingdom is reduced to the hills around Samaria.

properties.name: Sargon II — the fall of Samaria
properties.label: The fall of Samaria, 722 BCE

popup.bible: After three years of siege, Samaria falls; the northern kingdom is deported — the ten lost tribes (2 Kgs 17).
popup.archaeology: Sargon II claims the credit and the numbers: 'I conquered Samaria and carried away 27,290 people.' The destruction layer at Samaria is real. Israel ends.

popup.bible: 'In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them' (2 Kgs 18:13).
popup.archaeology: Sennacherib's prism: 46 walled cities taken, Lachish stormed (its reliefs adorn his palace), and Hezekiah 'shut up like a bird in a cage.' Jerusalem survives — the text and the stone agree on that much.

properties.name: Necho II — the march north, 609 BCE
properties.label: Pharaoh Necho, 609 BCE

popup.bible: Josiah marches out to stop Pharaoh Necho — and is killed at Megiddo (2 Kgs 23:29). The reformer's golden age dies with him.
popup.archaeology: Necho marches north to save the dying Assyrian remnant from Babylon. Josiah dies at Megiddo in 609 — the battlefield that keeps taking kings.

popup.bible: Jehoiachin surrenders; the king, the officials, the warriors, the craftsmen — about 10,000 people — are carried off (2 Kgs 24:14-16).
popup.archaeology: The Babylonian Chronicle BM 21946 records it in a month-and-day: 'He encamped against the city of Judah and on the second day of Adar he captured the city and seized its king.'

popup.bible: Eighteen months of siege. The walls breach, the city burns, the temple falls, the king is blinded (2 Kgs 25).
popup.archaeology: The Babylonian destruction layer at Jerusalem is unmistakable: ash, arrowheads, burned houses. The city that Yahweh protected from Assyria, Babylon ends.

properties.name: Cyrus — the conquest and the return
properties.label: Cyrus takes Babylon, 539 BCE

popup.bible: The Lord stirs up Cyrus — and the exiles are told they can go home (2 Chr 36:22-23; Ezra 1).
popup.archaeology: Cyrus diverts the Euphrates and walks into Babylon. The Cyrus Cylinder announces the restoration policy. The exile ends not with a miracle but an empire's administrative decision.

popup.bible: Sheshbazzar leads the first wave home with the temple vessels (Ezra 1:8-11). The priests return as a 'priesthood in waiting.'
popup.archaeology: Only a fraction returns — many stay in Babylon, where a Jewish community thrives for a millennium. The returnees carry the scrolls; the scrolls carry the new theology.
